tier_reason: The only numbers are in rust_xlsxwriter's src/performance.rs, written by the same author as both libxlsxwriter and the Python XlsxWriter baseline: hyperfine output (C 210.9 ms vs Python 919.1 ms, table 'Relative to C' 4.36) with the three test programs listed, but no compiler, flags, CPU model or Python version, so first-party with partial methodology, tier C.

corrections.caveats: The only numbers found are in the sister project rust_xlsxwriter's documentation (src/performance.rs), written by the same author as libxlsxwriter and as the Python XlsxWriter baseline, so first-party and tier C. The page lists the C, Rust and Python test programs and the hyperfine command (warmup 3), and its table states Python at 4.36 relative to C directly; compiler, flags, CPU model, Python version and libxlsxwriter build options are not stated. One small workload (200,000 unformatted cells, 4,000 rows x 50 columns), timed as whole-process wall time, so Python interpreter startup and import are included in the 919.1 ms; the Python program writes the integer 12345 where the C program writes 12345.0 (negligible). The comparison is cross-language (C library vs a pure-Python library), and libxlsxwriter loses to rust_xlsxwriter built with its zlib feature (152.6 ms; C is 1.38x slower) while beating plain rust_xlsxwriter (240.8 ms). The libxlsxwriter repo and its docs carry no benchmark of their own: docs/src/working_with_memory.dox and License.txt only say the bundled emyg_dtoa (Milo Yip dtoa) is 40-50 percent faster than the standard sprintf-based conversion for raw numeric data, with no numbers, and that library is optional and off by default (USE_DTOA_LIBRARY=1). Licence file is the FreeBSD variant of BSD-2-Clause (extra non-binding 'views and conclusions' sentence, SPDX BSD-2-Clause-Views); bundled optional parts are minizip (Zlib), tmpfileplus (MPL-2.0), emyg_dtoa (MIT), Openwall MD5 (public domain) and FreeBSD queue.h/tree.h (BSD). Commits of 2026-07-07 fixed a heap overflow with 256+ item data validation lists and quadratic memory use in default table columns; neither is on the benchmarked path. Corroborating but indirect: the Impeller README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/m9psy/Impeller/HEAD/README.md) reports a Cython wrapper over a modified fork of libxlsxwriter at 4.69 s total vs Python XlsxWriter 18.17 s for 100,000 x 10 cells on Windows, crude results from misc/simple_bench.py, which measures the fork, not upstream.

notes: Numbers verified on src/performance.rs (152.6 / 210.9 / 240.8 / 919.1 ms; table 4.36 relative to C). Shortcomings: first-party (same author owns baseline and sister projects), no compiler/flags/CPU/Python version, single 200k-cell workload with process startup included, cross-language baseline, slower than rust_xlsxwriter+zlib; dtoa 40-50 percent claim has no numbers and the library is off by default. Metadata checked: 1.8k stars, not fork or archived, last commit 2026-07-07, active; licence is the FreeBSD BSD-2-Clause variant (operative terms equal BSD-2-Clause, kept copyable).

tier_reason: Independent measurement by the Deepparse authors: the docs table (libpostal ~0.00004 s/address vs fastText ~0.0004 s GPU and ~0.0026 s CPU) is backed by public code (models_evaluation/speed_test_evaluation_libpostal.py and speed_test_evaluation.py) and, per search snippets, by Tables 1-2 of their peer-reviewed NLP-OSS 2023 paper (RTX 2080 GPU); not A because the CPU model and libpostal build are unstated and the committed Deepparse timing script does not run as written.

corrections.caveats: Independent measurement by the Deepparse authors (competitors, not the libpostal team). The numbers are in Deepparse's docs (docs/source/parser.rst); that page does not cite a paper for the timing tables (its arXiv link, 2006.16152, is the 2020 accuracy paper). Search snippets (snippet only; arXiv and ACL Anthology blocked) say the NLP-OSS 2023 paper 'Deepparse: An Extendable, and Fine-Tunable State-Of-The-Art Library for Parsing Multinational Street Addresses' (arXiv 2311.11846, ACL Anthology 2023.nlposs-1.3) reports the same experiment in Tables 1-2 on an RTX 2080 GPU and states that libpostal had the better inference time. The benchmark code is public in GRAAL-Research/deepparse models_evaluation/: libpostal was timed through the pypostal Python binding (postal.parser.parse_address in a Python loop over ~183,000 addresses, wall-clock time.time()), not from C, and both runs are wrapped in memory_profiler's @profile, whose line tracing adds overhead to the libpostal loop, so the libpostal figure is if anything pessimistic. The committed speed_test_evaluation.py calls process_fn() without its batch_size argument and reopens its result file inside the batch loop, so it cannot have produced the Deepparse rows as written; its 'batch of more than 1' column is the mean over batch sizes 2 to 512, not the best batch. The CPU model, libpostal version, data model and build flags are not stated (run 2023-03-21: Linux, Python 3.11, Torch 2.0, CUDA 11.7). The libpostal row has a single number (repeated in the GPU and CPU tables; RAM and batch-1 cells are N/A), so ratios against Deepparse's batch-of-1 column are not like for like. Off-baseline: Deepparse (353 stars, LGPL-3.0) is a neural parser aimed at accuracy on noisy multinational addresses, not an incumbent; libpostal is itself the incumbent for address parsing, and its own README claims 10-30k addresses per second per thread with a simple benchmark program but publishes no comparison. 0.00004 s per address equals 25,000 addresses per second (derived from page data), consistent with that README claim. Category fit is loose: address parsing and normalization filed under text-search-and-indexing.

notes: Numbers verified on parser.rst (libpostal ~0.00004 s; fastText GPU 0.0023/0.0004, CPU 0.0128/0.0026; BPEmbAttention CPU batch-1 0.0286). Shortcomings: off-baseline (Deepparse is a niche neural competitor, not an incumbent), libpostal timed via pypostal Python binding under memory_profiler, CPU model and libpostal build unstated, committed Deepparse speed script broken (process_fn() missing argument), paper only via search snippets, loose category. Metadata checked: MIT, 4.9k stars, not fork or archived, last commit 2025-12-06, active.
